claim: Myofibers are the main components of skeletal muscle, which is the largest tissue in the body.
source: Myofibers are the main components of skeletal muscle, which is the largest tissue in the body.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge about skeletal muscle composition.

claim: Myofibers are highly adaptive and can be altered under different biological and disease conditions.
source: Myofibers are highly adaptive and can be altered under different biological and disease conditions.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about muscle fiber plasticity.

claim: Single-cell sequencing has permitted the study of the epigenome of isolated myonuclei.
source: Single-cell sequencing has permitted the study of the epigenome of isolated myonuclei.
evidence: This is a statement about existing technology capabilities in the field.

claim: Single-cell sequencing provides sequencing with high dimensionality but the sequencing depth is lacking.
source: While this provides sequencing with high dimensionality, the sequencing depth is lacking, which makes comparisons between different biological conditions difficult.
evidence: This is a known limitation of single-cell sequencing technologies.

claim: This study reports the first implementation of single myofiber ATAC-Seq.
source: Here, we report the first implementation of single myofiber ATAC-Seq, which allows for the sequencing of an individual myofiber at a depth sufficient for peak calling and for comparative analysis of chromatin accessibility under various physiological and disease conditions.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the method presented in this manuscript.

claim: Single myofiber ATAC-Seq allows for sequencing of an individual myofiber at a depth sufficient for peak calling.
source: Here, we report the first implementation of single myofiber ATAC-Seq, which allows for the sequencing of an individual myofiber at a depth sufficient for peak calling and for comparative analysis of chromatin accessibility under various physiological and disease conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data presented in the manuscript showing approximately 6 million final reads aligned and 30,000 peaks called.

claim: Application of single myofiber ATAC-Seq revealed significant differences in chromatin accessibility between resting and regenerating myofibers.
source: Application of this technique revealed significant differences in chromatin accessibility between resting and regenerating myofibers, as well as between myofibers from a mouse model of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (mdx) and wild-type (WT) counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by the differential analysis and comparative data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Application of single myofiber ATAC-Seq revealed significant differences in chromatin accessibility between myofibers from mdx mice and wild-type counterparts.
source: Application of this technique revealed significant differences in chromatin accessibility between resting and regenerating myofibers, as well as between myofibers from a mouse model of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (mdx) and wild-type (WT) counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by the differential analysis and comparative data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myofibers are formed from the fusion of myogenic precursor cells.
source: The main component of skeletal muscle are myofibers which are formed from the fusion of myogenic precursor cells (Buckingham et al., 2003) resulting in large postmitotic syncytia that are composed of repeating contractile units, called sarcomeres (Huxley and Hanson, 1954).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buckingham et al., 2003.

claim: Myofibers are large postmitotic syncytia composed of repeating contractile units called sarcomeres.
source: The main component of skeletal muscle are myofibers which are formed from the fusion of myogenic precursor cells (Buckingham et al., 2003) resulting in large postmitotic syncytia that are composed of repeating contractile units, called sarcomeres (Huxley and Hanson, 1954).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huxley and Hanson, 1954.

claim: Myofibers exhibit wide variations in their metabolic activity and contractile properties.
source: Myofibers exhibit wide variations in their metabolic activity and contractile properties (Zierath and Hawley, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zierath and Hawley, 2004.

claim: Myofiber characteristics are regulated by complex processes involving rates of protein turnover.
source: In addition, they have a highly adaptive nature where their size, myosin heavy chain isoform, energy metabolism, and the overall skeletal muscle mass, among other characteristics, are regulated by complex processes involving rates of protein turnover (Bohé et al., 2001; Mittendorfer et al., 2005), as well as transcriptional (Quiat et al., 2011) and posttranscriptional (Weskamp et al., 2021) control of gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bohé et al., 2001 and Mittendorfer et al., 2005.

claim: Myofiber characteristics are regulated by transcriptional control of gene expression.
source: In addition, they have a highly adaptive nature where their size, myosin heavy chain isoform, energy metabolism, and the overall skeletal muscle mass, among other characteristics, are regulated by complex processes involving rates of protein turnover (Bohé et al., 2001; Mittendorfer et al., 2005), as well as transcriptional (Quiat et al., 2011) and posttranscriptional (Weskamp et al., 2021) control of gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Quiat et al., 2011.

claim: Myofiber characteristics are regulated by posttranscriptional control of gene expression.
source: In addition, they have a highly adaptive nature where their size, myosin heavy chain isoform, energy metabolism, and the overall skeletal muscle mass, among other characteristics, are regulated by complex processes involving rates of protein turnover (Bohé et al., 2001; Mittendorfer et al., 2005), as well as transcriptional (Quiat et al., 2011) and posttranscriptional (Weskamp et al., 2021) control of gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weskamp et al., 2021.

claim: Myofibers can change in response to exercise.
source: Due to their adaptive nature, myofibers can change in response to exercise (Zierath and Hawley, 2004; Wilson et al., 2012; Dons et al., 1979), aging (Deschenes, 2004) and diseases, such as sarcopenia (Thompson, 2002; Nilwik et al., 2013) and cachexia (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zierath and Hawley, 2004; Wilson et al., 2012; Dons et al., 1979.

claim: Myofibers can change in response to aging.
source: Due to their adaptive nature, myofibers can change in response to exercise (Zierath and Hawley, 2004; Wilson et al., 2012; Dons et al., 1979), aging (Deschenes, 2004) and diseases, such as sarcopenia (Thompson, 2002; Nilwik et al., 2013) and cachexia (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deschenes, 2004.

claim: Myofibers can change in response to diseases such as sarcopenia.
source: Due to their adaptive nature, myofibers can change in response to exercise (Zierath and Hawley, 2004; Wilson et al., 2012; Dons et al., 1979), aging (Deschenes, 2004) and diseases, such as sarcopenia (Thompson, 2002; Nilwik et al., 2013) and cachexia (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thompson, 2002 and Nilwik et al., 2013.

claim: Myofibers can change in response to diseases such as cachexia.
source: Due to their adaptive nature, myofibers can change in response to exercise (Zierath and Hawley, 2004; Wilson et al., 2012; Dons et al., 1979), aging (Deschenes, 2004) and diseases, such as sarcopenia (Thompson, 2002; Nilwik et al., 2013) and cachexia (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roberts et al., 2013.

claim: Myofibers act as a key signaling component of muscle stem cells.
source: Myofibers also act as a key signaling component of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) (Lazure et al., 2020), which are in turn required for the regeneration of muscle fibers after injury (Snow, 1977; Shadrach and Wagers, 2011; Dumont et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lazure et al., 2020.

claim: Muscle stem cells are required for the regeneration of muscle fibers after injury.
source: Myofibers also act as a key signaling component of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) (Lazure et al., 2020), which are in turn required for the regeneration of muscle fibers after injury (Snow, 1977; Shadrach and Wagers, 2011; Dumont et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Snow, 1977; Shadrach and Wagers, 2011; Dumont et al., 2015.

claim: Skeletal muscle is a very heterogenous tissue composed of myofibers, associated MuSCs, and numerous different non-myogenic cell types.
source: Skeletal muscle is a very heterogenous tissue composed not only of myofibers and their associated MuSCs, but also numerous different non-myogenic cell types (Giordani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Giordani et al., 2019.

claim: Single nucleus RNA-Seq and single nucleus ATAC-Seq have analyzed the transcriptome and epigenome of myonuclei within muscle fiber.
source: Recent studies using these technologies to study muscle tissue, such as single nucleus RNA-Seq and single nucleus ATAC-Seq have analyzed the transcriptome and epigenome of the myonuclei within the muscle fiber (Petrany et al., 2020; Dos Santos et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Petrany et al., 2020; Dos Santos et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020.

claim: Single nucleus sequencing methods have low sequencing depth with limited capacity for downstream analyses.
source: However, they present certain limitations where they sequence all myonuclei present in the muscle and cannot distinguish between different myofibers, as well as having low sequencing depth with a limited capacity for downstream analyses.
evidence: This is a known limitation of single nucleus sequencing technologies.

claim: The chromatin state plays a key role in transcriptional regulation and the determination of cellular identity.
source: The chromatin state plays a key role in transcriptional regulation and the determination of cellular identity (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2018.

claim: Accessible regions make up only 3% of the total genome but represent over 90% of known transcription factor binding sites.
source: Although the accessible regions make up only 3% of the total genome, it represents over 90% of known transcription factor binding sites (Thurman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thurman et al., 2012.

claim: Chromatin accessibility is a determinant of gene expression.
source: Chromatin accessibility is a determinant of gene expression, and changes in chromatin accessibility have been identified in different biological and disease conditions such as during development (Liu et al., 2019a; Trevino et al., 2020), cancers (Corces et al., 2018; Rendeiro et al., 2016), and neurological disorders (Wang et al., 2020; Bastle and Maze, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of epigenetics.

claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility have been identified during development.
source: Chromatin accessibility is a determinant of gene expression, and changes in chromatin accessibility have been identified in different biological and disease conditions such as during development (Liu et al., 2019a; Trevino et al., 2020), cancers (Corces et al., 2018; Rendeiro et al., 2016), and neurological disorders (Wang et al., 2020; Bastle and Maze, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2019a and Trevino et al., 2020.

claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility have been identified in cancers.
source: Chromatin accessibility is a determinant of gene expression, and changes in chromatin accessibility have been identified in different biological and disease conditions such as during development (Liu et al., 2019a; Trevino et al., 2020), cancers (Corces et al., 2018; Rendeiro et al., 2016), and neurological disorders (Wang et al., 2020; Bastle and Maze, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Corces et al., 2018 and Rendeiro et al., 2016.

claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility have been identified in neurological disorders.
source: Chromatin accessibility is a determinant of gene expression, and changes in chromatin accessibility have been identified in different biological and disease conditions such as during development (Liu et al., 2019a; Trevino et al., 2020), cancers (Corces et al., 2018; Rendeiro et al., 2016), and neurological disorders (Wang et al., 2020; Bastle and Maze, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020 and Bastle and Maze, 2019.

claim: ATAC-Seq relies on the hyperactive Tn5 transposase that fragments accessible regions in the genome while simultaneously ligating sequencing compatible adaptors.
source: ATAC-Seq relies on the hyperactive Tn5 transposase that fragments the accessible regions in the genome while simultaneously ligating sequencing compatible adaptors (Corces et al., 2017; Buenrostro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Corces et al., 2017 and Buenrostro et al., 2015.

claim: ATAC-Seq has been applied to many different cell types and tissues.
source: Over the years, ATAC-Seq has been applied to many different cell types and tissues (Liu et al., 2019b; Yan et al., 2020; Rocks et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2019b; Yan et al., 2020; Rocks et al., 2022.

claim: ATAC-Seq has not been performed on a single myofiber prior to this study.
source: However, to our knowledge, it has not been performed on a single myofiber, possibly due to the rigidity of their membrane, high levels of mitochondria (Janssen et al., 2000; Ortenblad et al., 2018; Mishra et al., 2015), and the low number of myonuclei that are present in a single myofiber (Neal et al., 2012; Cramer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Myofibers have high levels of mitochondria.
source: However, to our knowledge, it has not been performed on a single myofiber, possibly due to the rigidity of their membrane, high levels of mitochondria (Janssen et al., 2000; Ortenblad et al., 2018; Mishra et al., 2015), and the low number of myonuclei that are present in a single myofiber (Neal et al., 2012; Cramer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janssen et al., 2000; Ortenblad et al., 2018; Mishra et al., 2015.

claim: A single myofiber has a low number of myonuclei.
source: However, to our knowledge, it has not been performed on a single myofiber, possibly due to the rigidity of their membrane, high levels of mitochondria (Janssen et al., 2000; Ortenblad et al., 2018; Mishra et al., 2015), and the low number of myonuclei that are present in a single myofiber (Neal et al., 2012; Cramer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neal et al., 2012 and Cramer et al., 2020.

claim: This study adapted OMNI-ATAC-seq to determine the genome-wide chromatin accessibility of myonuclei contained within a single EDL muscle fiber of a mouse.
source: Here, we have adapted OMNI-ATAC-seq to determine the genome-wide chromatin accessibility of myonuclei contained within a single Extensor Digitorum Longus (EDL) muscle fiber of a mouse.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed in this study.

claim: The smfATAC-Seq method allows for investigation of accessible chromatin regions of a single myofiber without the presence of other confounding cell types.
source: The single myofiber ATAC-Seq (smfATAC-Seq) method that we applied in this study allows for the investigation of the accessible chromatin regions of a single myofiber, without the presence of other confounding cell types.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing absence of peaks at non-myogenic cell markers.

claim: The smfATAC-Seq has a sequencing depth of approximately 6 million final reads aligned.
source: The smfATAC-Seq has a sequencing depth of approximately 6 million final reads aligned which provides approximately 30,000 peaks called.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: The smfATAC-Seq provides approximately 30,000 peaks called.
source: The smfATAC-Seq has a sequencing depth of approximately 6 million final reads aligned which provides approximately 30,000 peaks called.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: This study provides comparative analysis of chromatin accessibility between resting and regenerating myofibers.
source: Using this method, we provide comparative analysis of chromatin accessibility between resting and regenerating myofibers, as well as their MuSC progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by the differential analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Application of smfATAC-Seq to mdx mice provides a genome-wide assessment of changes in chromatin accessibility in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.
source: In addition, application of this method to the study of myofibers isolated from a mouse model of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (mdx) (McGreevy et al., 2015) and their WT counterparts provide a genome-wide assessment of changes in chromatin accessibility in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis data between mdx and WT myofibers.

claim: A single EDL myofiber of a mouse contains an average of 200-300 myonuclei.
source: A single EDL myofiber of a mouse contains an average of 200–300 myonuclei (Neal et al., 2012; Cramer et al., 2020), making genome-wide analyses of the chromatin state difficult.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neal et al., 2012 and Cramer et al., 2020.

claim: Analysis of chromatin accessibility of samples with an input of as low as 500 cells is now possible with OMNI ATAC-Seq.
source: With the advancements in next generation sequencing (NGS) and the development of the OMNI ATAC-Seq protocol (Corces et al., 2017), analysis of chromatin accessibility of samples with an input of as low as 500 cells is now possible (Corces et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Corces et al., 2017.

claim: Only 0.9-2.09% of reads were derived from mitochondria in smfATAC-Seq.
source: Furthermore, analysis showed that only 0.9–2.09% of reads were derived from the mitochondria in smfATAC-Seq (Table 1), suggesting that this method is highly efficient for the removal of mitochondria from mitochondria-rich myofibers.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: The smfATAC-Seq method is highly efficient for the removal of mitochondria from mitochondria-rich myofibers.
source: Furthermore, analysis showed that only 0.9–2.09% of reads were derived from the mitochondria in smfATAC-Seq (Table 1), suggesting that this method is highly efficient for the removal of mitochondria from mitochondria-rich myofibers.
evidence: This is inferred from the low percentage of mitochondrial reads shown in Table 1.

claim: Following removal of mitochondrial reads, there were approximately 6 million final reads aligned and 30,000 peaks called.
source: Following the removal of mitochondrial reads, there were approximately 6 million final reads aligned and 30,000 peaks called, demonstrating a sufficient sequencing depth for downstream analysis (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: DNA fragment sizes obtained from smfATAC-Seq were of a similar range in size as those obtained from conventional OMNI ATAC-Seq performed on 5000 MuSCs.
source: DNA fragment sizes obtained from the smfATAC-Seq were of a similar range in size as those obtained from conventional OMNI ATAC-Seq which we have performed on 5000 MuSCs that were freshly isolated by Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer profiles shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 0.1% of the peaks in smfATAC-Seq overlapped with the top 100 non-fiber muscle genes.
source: We determined the number of peaks in smfATAC-Seq that overlap with non-fiber muscle genes, which revealed that only 0.1% of the peaks overlapped with the top 100 non-fiber muscle genes (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 2.

claim: 0.33% of the peaks in whole EDL muscle ATAC-Seq overlapped with the top 100 non-fiber muscle genes.
source: In comparison, 0.33% of the peaks in the whole EDL muscle ATAC-Seq (GSM3981673) (Ramachandran et al., 2019) overlapped with the top 100 non-fiber muscle genes (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 2 and comparison with published data from Ramachandran et al., 2019.

claim: The significant difference in overlap with non-fiber muscle genes between whole muscle ATAC-Seq and smfATAC-Seq suggests that whole muscle ATAC-Seq has enrichment of peaks associated with non-myogenic genes.
source: The significant difference in the overlap with the non-fiber muscle genes between the whole muscle ATAC-Seq and smfATAC-Seq suggest that the whole muscle ATAC-Seq has enrichment of peaks associated with non-myogenic genes when compared to the smfATAC-Seq, which implies that smfATAC-Seq can successfully exclude the non-myogenic cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis of peak overlaps.

claim: smfATAC-Seq can successfully exclude non-myogenic cell types.
source: The significant difference in the overlap with the non-fiber muscle genes between the whole muscle ATAC-Seq and smfATAC-Seq suggest that the whole muscle ATAC-Seq has enrichment of peaks associated with non-myogenic genes when compared to the smfATAC-Seq, which implies that smfATAC-Seq can successfully exclude the non-myogenic cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis and supported by absence of peaks at non-myogenic markers.

claim: None of the non-myogenic cell marker genes had ATAC-Seq peaks at their promoters in smfATAC-Seq samples.
source: None of these marker genes had ATAC-Seq peaks at their promoters, indicating that only a single myofiber is processed without any other contaminating cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the IGV snapshots shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Damaged or regenerating myofibers can be visualized by their characteristic feature of centrally located nuclei.
source: Damaged or regenerating myofibers can be visualized by their characteristic feature of centrally located nuclei (Roman and Gomes, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roman and Gomes, 2018.

claim: Injured myofibers were visually selected for the presence of centrally located myonuclei by Hoechst staining.
source: Injured myofibers in this method were visually selected for the presence of the centrally located myonuclei by Hoechst staining and the selected myofiber was used for downstream processing with smfATAC-Seq (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the images shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: More than half of the peaks in MuSCs were in intron/distal intergenic regions (enhancer regions) and about 25% were in the promoter region.
source: Peak annotation analysis for MuSCs revealed that more than half of the peaks were in the intron/distal intergenic regions (i.e. enhancer regions) and about 25% of the peaks were in the promoter region (Figure 2C, Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and Table 4.

claim: Peak annotations for uninjured and injured single myofibers showed a great proportion of peaks in the enhancer and promoter regions.
source: Peak annotations for the uninjured and injured single myofibers also showed a great proportion of peaks in the enhancer and promoter regions (Figure 2D and E, Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D, E and Table 4.

claim: An enrichment of ATAC-seq reads around Transcription Start Sites (±1 kb) from all datasets was observed.
source: In addition, an enrichment of ATAC-seq reads around Transcription Start Sites (TSS) (±1 kb) from all datasets was observed, which is a typical result that is expected from ATAC-Seq (Yan et al., 2020) (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmaps shown in Figure 2F-H and is a known characteristic of ATAC-Seq data.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks were present in the promoter regions of Ckm, Acta1, Myf6, and Myh4 in myofiber samples.
source: For instance, in the myofiber samples, we confirmed the presence of ATAC-seq peaks in the promoter regions of Ckm, Actin alpha 1 (Acta1), Myogenic factor 6 (Myf6), and Myosin heavy chain 4 (Myh4), all of which are expressed by myofibers but not MuSCs (Lazure et al., 2020; Tai et al., 2011; Nowak et al., 1999; Stuart et al., 2016) (Figure 2I–L).
evidence: This is supported by the IGV snapshots shown in Figure 2I-L and citations to literature showing these genes are expressed in myofibers.

claim: Ckm, Acta1, Myf6, and Myh4 are expressed by myofibers but not MuSCs.
source: For instance, in the myofiber samples, we confirmed the presence of ATAC-seq peaks in the promoter regions of Ckm, Actin alpha 1 (Acta1), Myogenic factor 6 (Myf6), and Myosin heavy chain 4 (Myh4), all of which are expressed by myofibers but not MuSCs (Lazure et al., 2020; Tai et al., 2011; Nowak et al., 1999; Stuart et al., 2016) (Figure 2I–L).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lazure et al., 2020; Tai et al., 2011; Nowak et al., 1999; Stuart et al., 2016.

claim: Peaks were observed in the promoter regions of Pax7 and Myf5 in MuSCs.
source: On the other hand, in MuSCs we observed peaks in the promoter regions of Paired Box 7 (Pax7), and Myf5, genes that are known to be expressed in MuSCs (Rudnicki et al., 1993; Seale et al., 2000) (Figure 2M–N).
evidence: This is supported by the IGV snapshots shown in Figure 2M-N and citations showing these genes are expressed in MuSCs.

claim: Pax7 and Myf5 are known to be expressed in MuSCs.
source: On the other hand, in MuSCs we observed peaks in the promoter regions of Paired Box 7 (Pax7), and Myf5, genes that are known to be expressed in MuSCs (Rudnicki et al., 1993; Seale et al., 2000) (Figure 2M–N).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rudnicki et al., 1993 and Seale et al., 2000.

claim: Muscle regeneration and repair rely on the temporal expression of Myogenic Regulatory Factors (MRFs): Myf5, MyoD, Myog, and Myf6/MRF4.
source: Muscle regeneration and repair rely on the temporal expression of Myogenic Regulatory Factors (MRFs), Myf5, MyoD, Myog, and Myf6/MRF4 (Hernández-Hernández et al., 2017; Montarras et al., 1991; Asfour et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hernández-Hernández et al., 2017; Montarras et al., 1991; Asfour et al., 2018.

claim: Peaks in the promoter regions of Myf5 were observed only in MuSCs but not in myofibers.
source: We observed peaks in the promoter regions of Myf5 only in the MuSCs but not in the myofibers and peaks in the promoters of Myog and Myf6/MRF4 were solely observed in the myofibers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the IGV snapshots shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Peaks in the promoters of Myog and Myf6/MRF4 were solely observed in myofibers.
source: We observed peaks in the promoter regions of Myf5 only in the MuSCs but not in the myofibers and peaks in the promoters of Myog and Myf6/MRF4 were solely observed in the myofibers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the IGV snapshots shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Peaks in the promoter regions of MyoD were observed in both MuSCs and myofibers.
source: However, we observed peaks in the promoter regions of MyoD in both the MuSCs and myofibers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the IGV snapshots shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Biological replicates within conditions are more similar to one another than to those from other conditions.
source: To show the global differences in chromatin accessibility between MuSCs, uninjured and injured myofibers, we first performed heatmap clustering of Pearson correlation coefficients on all the replicates/samples, which shows that the biological replicates within conditions are more similar to one another than to those from the other conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Each condition clusters separately in PCA analysis, with injured and uninjured myofibers being more similar to one another than to MuSCs.
source: This can also be observed through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) where each condition clusters separately, with the injured and uninjured myofibers being more similar to one another than to MuSCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA plot shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Uninjured and injured myofibers cluster separately when analyzed without MuSCs.
source: To test whether the differences between regenerating and resting myofibers are overshadowed by their differences with MuSCs, we performed heatmap clustering of Pearson correlation coefficients and PCA analysis for injured and uninjured myofibers only, without MuSCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). This further highlighted how the uninjured and injured myofibers cluster separately (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Troponin I2 (Tnni2) and Troponin T3 (Tnnt3) are markers of fast fiber types.
source: Troponin I2 (Tnni2) and Troponin T3 (Tnnt3), markers of fast fiber types, (Mullen and Barton, 2000; Wei and Jin, 2016) had a high level of chromatin accessibility while Troponin T1 (Tnnt1) and Myosin heavy chain 7 (Myh7), which are expressed in slow fiber types displayed no chromatin accessibility (Wei and Jin, 2016; Meredith et al., 2004) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mullen and Barton, 2000 and Wei and Jin, 2016.

claim: Tnni2 and Tnnt3 had a high level of chromatin accessibility in the analyzed myofibers.
source: Troponin I2 (Tnni2) and Troponin T3 (Tnnt3), markers of fast fiber types, (Mullen and Barton, 2000; Wei and Jin, 2016) had a high level of chromatin accessibility while Troponin T1 (Tnnt1) and Myosin heavy chain 7 (Myh7), which are expressed in slow fiber types displayed no chromatin accessibility (Wei and Jin, 2016; Meredith et al., 2004) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the IGV snapshots shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Troponin T1 (Tnnt1) and Myosin heavy chain 7 (Myh7) are expressed in slow fiber types.
source: Troponin I2 (Tnni2) and Troponin T3 (Tnnt3), markers of fast fiber types, (Mullen and Barton, 2000; Wei and Jin, 2016) had a high level of chromatin accessibility while Troponin T1 (Tnnt1) and Myosin heavy chain 7 (Myh7), which are expressed in slow fiber types displayed no chromatin accessibility (Wei and Jin, 2016; Meredith et al., 2004) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wei and Jin, 2016 and Meredith et al., 2004.

claim: Tnnt1 and Myh7 displayed no chromatin accessibility in the analyzed myofibers.
source: Troponin I2 (Tnni2) and Troponin T3 (Tnnt3), markers of fast fiber types, (Mullen and Barton, 2000; Wei and Jin, 2016) had a high level of chromatin accessibility while Troponin T1 (Tnnt1) and Myosin heavy chain 7 (Myh7), which are expressed in slow fiber types displayed no chromatin accessibility (Wei and Jin, 2016; Meredith et al., 2004) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the IGV snapshots shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only fast fiber types were analyzed in this study.
source: This data indicates that only fast fiber types were analyzed in this study and that the differences in the chromatin state between the injured and uninjured myofibers were not due to the differences in the fiber types.
evidence: This is inferred from the chromatin accessibility patterns of fiber type markers.

claim: The differences in chromatin state between injured and uninjured myofibers were not due to differences in fiber types.
source: This data indicates that only fast fiber types were analyzed in this study and that the differences in the chromatin state between the injured and uninjured myofibers were not due to the differences in the fiber types.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis showing all samples were fast fiber type.

claim: The differential peaks between uninjured myofibers and MuSCs were mostly found close to the promoter region (≤1 kb).
source: For instance, the differential peaks between uninjured myofibers and MuSCs were mostly found close to the promoter region ( ≤ 1 kb), whereas in the uninjured and injured myofibers comparison, a greater proportion of differential peaks were found in the intron/distal intergenic regions (i.e. enhancer regions) (Figure 3E, Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3E and Table 5.

claim: In the uninjured and injured myofibers comparison, a greater proportion of differential peaks were found in intron/distal intergenic regions (enhancer regions).

claim: Striated muscle cell development, actomyosin structure, and sarcomere organization are important for myofiber structural formation and proper function.

evidence: This is established knowledge about muscle biology.

claim: Genes associated with nearest unique peaks from injured myofibers mostly belong to processes involved in structural components of the myofiber.

claim: Genes associated with nearest unique peaks from uninjured myofibers correspond to genes involved in ion transport and metabolism.

claim: GSEA between uninjured and injured myofibers revealed that inflammatory response and Il2-Stat5 signaling pathways are still operational even after 7 days of CTX-mediated injury to muscle.
source: Importantly, the GSEA between uninjured and injured myofibers revealed that inflammatory response and Il2-Stat5 signaling, and injury related pathways are still operational even after 7 days of CTX-mediated injury to muscle (Laurence et al., 2007) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the GSEA results shown in Figure 5A and citation to literature.

source: The GSEA between uninjured myofibers and MuSCs revealed that one of the significantly enriched pathways is myogenesis, where we can observe that genes associated with differentiation and myofiber function such as Myf6, Ckm,and Tropomyosin 2 (Tpm2) (Lazure et al., 2020; Tai et al., 2011; Buckingham, 1994; Jin et al., 2016) have higher accessibility in the myofiber compared to MuSCs (Figure 5B-D).

claim: Myf6, Ckm, and Tpm2 are associated with differentiation and myofiber function.
source: The GSEA between uninjured myofibers and MuSCs revealed that one of the significantly enriched pathways is myogenesis, where we can observe that genes associated with differentiation and myofiber function such as Myf6, Ckm,and Tropomyosin 2 (Tpm2) (Lazure et al., 2020; Tai et al., 2011; Buckingham, 1994; Jin et al., 2016) have higher accessibility in the myofiber compared to MuSCs (Figure 5B-D).

claim: Myf6, Ckm, and Tpm2 have higher accessibility in myofiber compared to MuSCs.

evidence: This is supported by the heatmap and IGV snapshots shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Genes associated with quiescence and MuSCs such as Itga7 and Gpx3 are more accessible in MuSCs compared to myofiber.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Bjornson et al., 2012; Mourikis and Tajbakhsh, 2014; Carlson et al., 2009; Girardi et al., 2021.

claim: For TGFβ signalling, Noggin shows more accessibility in myofibers while Bmp4 has increased accessibility in MuSCs.

claim: smfATAC-Seq is an effective method to analyze chromatin accessibility and to identify active cis-regulatory elements in a single muscle fiber.
source: Taken together, this data shows that smfATAC-Seq is an effective method to analyze chromatin accessibility and to identify active cis-regulatory elements in a single muscle fiber as well as to compare muscle fibers under different physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: smfATAC-Seq can be used to compare muscle fibers under different physiological conditions.
source: Taken together, this data shows that smfATAC-Seq is an effective method to analyze chromatin accessibility and to identify active cis-regulatory elements in a single muscle fiber as well as to compare muscle fibers under different physiological conditions.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Myofibers that were not actively regenerating were selected for processing from both mdx and WT conditions.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental design to control for regeneration effects.

evidence: This is supported by the heatmaps shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Most of the peaks in mdx and WT myofibers were in the promoter and enhancer regions.

evidence: This is supported by the heatmap and PCA plot shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: mdx and WT myofibers exhibit extensive differences in their chromatin states.

The results clearly showed that mdx and WT myofibers exhibit extensive differences in their chromatin states (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the pile-up analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: More than half of the differential peaks between mdx and WT myofibers were found in enhancer regions.

evidence: This is supported by the peak annotation pie chart shown in Figure 6F and data in Table 5.

claim: mdx and WT myofibers differ mostly at the level of distal regulatory elements.
source: Peak annotation analysis on the differential peaks between mdx and WT myofibers revealed that more than half of the differential peaks were found in enhancer regions, indicating that they differ mostly at the level of distal regulatory elements (Figure 6F, Table 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the peak annotation analysis.

claim: Mitochondrial transport, myofibril assembly, sarcomere organization, and striated muscle cell development are important for myofiber structure, organization, and function.

These analyses revealed processes involved in mitochondrial transport, myofibril assembly, sarcomere organization, and striated muscle cell development, which are important for myofiber structure, organization, and function (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).

claim: smfATAC-Seq can be reliably used to study myofibers in disease conditions.

evidence: This is supported by the differential analysis and comparative data between mdx and WT myofibers.

claim: Single nucleus RNA-Seq and single nucleus ATAC-Seq sequence all myonuclei present in muscle and cannot distinguish between different myofibers.
source: To overcome this limitation, single nucleus RNA-Seq (snRNA-Seq) and single nucleus ATAC-Seq (snATAC-Seq) have been developed and performed on myonuclei to allow for the computational removal of other cell types (Petrany et al., 2020; Dos Santos et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020). However, these methods still sequence all myonuclei present in the muscle and cannot distinguish between different myofibers within a muscle.
evidence: This is a known limitation of single nucleus sequencing methods.

claim: snATAC-Seq is limited in sequencing depth due to generation of sparse reads.
source: Although snATAC-Seq provides high dimensionality, it is limited in sequencing depth due to the generation of sparse reads.
evidence: This is a known limitation of single nucleus ATAC-Seq technology.

claim: Computational pseudo bulking of snATAC-Seq can increase read numbers for comparative analysis but the pooled reads represent the average of all myonuclei within the sample.
source: Although computational pseudo bulking of snATAC-Seq can increase read numbers for comparative analysis between samples and conditions, the pooled reads represent the average of all myonuclei within the sample.
evidence: This is a known characteristic and limitation of pseudo-bulking approaches.

claim: This study introduces a highly effective protocol based on adaptation of OMNI ATAC-Seq to quantify chromatin accessibility of a single EDL myofiber with high resolution and sequencing depth.
source: In this study, we have introduced a highly effective protocol based on the adaption of OMNI ATAC-Seq (Corces et al., 2017) to quantify chromatin accessibility of a single EDL myofiber with high resolution and sequencing depth.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The smfATAC-Seq protocol investigates the open chromatin state of myofibers at a single myofiber resolution with high sequencing depth that allows for peak calling and differential peak analysis.
source: The smfATAC-Seq protocol that we introduce in this study investigates the open chromatin state of myofibers at a single myofiber resolution, and with a high sequencing depth that allows for peak calling and differential peak analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data showing sufficient depth for peak calling and differential analysis.

claim: smfATAC-Seq strictly investigates a single myofiber without the confounding presence of muscle resident non-myogenic cell types.
source: In this study, we have also demonstrated that smfATAC-Seq strictly investigates a single myofiber without the confounding presence of muscle resident non-myogenic cell types.
evidence: This is supported by the absence of peaks at non-myogenic cell markers.

claim: Application of trypsin to isolated myofibers effectively removes MuSCs that are associated with myofibers.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Blackburn et al., 2019 and confirmed by absence of peaks at MuSC markers.

claim: All smfATAC-Seq samples sequenced in this study were fast type myofibers.
source: Although all the smfATAC-Seq samples sequenced in this study were fast type myofibers, this protocol can be used to distinguish between different fiber types which could be applied to study myofiber heterogeneity under various physiological conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the chromatin accessibility patterns of fiber type markers.

claim: The smfATAC-Seq protocol can be used to distinguish between different fiber types.
source: Although all the smfATAC-Seq samples sequenced in this study were fast type myofibers, this protocol can be used to distinguish between different fiber types which could be applied to study myofiber heterogeneity under various physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the method.

claim: smfATAC-Seq is a robust technique to investigate genome-wide chromatin accessibility of a single myofiber.
source: smfATAC-Seq peaks associated with genes involved in muscle structure and function such as Acta1, Ckm and the myosin heavy chain cluster, indicates that our smfATAC-Seq is a robust technique to investigate genome-wide chromatin accessibility of a single myofiber.
evidence: This is supported by the presence of peaks at known muscle-specific genes.

claim: There are major modifications to chromatin accessibility in the context of regeneration.
source: In addition, through occupancy analysis, we showed that there is a large difference in the number of unique peaks present in the injured myofibers compared to uninjured myofibers. This indicates that there are major modifications to chromatin accessibility in the context of regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the occupancy analysis showing large differences in unique peaks.

claim: The similarity in biological processes between injured and uninjured fibers despite differences in chromatin profile may suggest activation of multiple enhancers on core muscle structural genes in the case of injury.
source: Despite these similarities, there are certain trends in which uninjured myofibers have increased accessibility in genes involved in energy metabolism, while injured myofibers have greater accessibility in genes involved in myogenesis and inflammatory response which is what would be expected in the case of an injury and regeneration (Tidball, 2011). Despite the increase in chromatin accessibility during injury, the accessible chromatin regions in both injured and uninjured fibers are associated with genes involved in similar biological processes. This similarity at the gene network despite differences in chromatin profile may suggest activation of multiple enhancers on core muscle structural genes in the case of injury.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data patterns.

claim: It is possible that harvesting injured EDL myofibers 7 days post injury allowed these myofibers to return to a state reminiscent of homeostatic myofibers.
source: Another possible reason could be the length of the recovery time where at 7 days post injury, a number of genes activated early in the regeneration process may have returned to levels seen in the steady state. Previously, a study investigating the changes in the transcriptional profile of MuSCs and various muscle resident cells throughout different time points of muscle injury using single cell RNA-Seq, revealed that after seven days of regeneration most cell types returned to a state that was similar to homeostasis (De Micheli et al., 2020a). Therefore, it is possible that harvesting the injured EDL myofibers 7 days post injury allowed these myofibers to return to a state reminiscent of homeostatic myofibers.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to De Micheli et al., 2020a showing cells return to homeostatic state after 7 days.

claim: The regions of open chromatin in myofibers correspond to genes involved in structural components of the muscle such as the z-disc.
source: We have also used smfATAC-Seq to compare changes in chromatin accessibility between MuSCs and myofibers. Our data shows that the regions of open chromatin in the myofibers correspond to genes involved in structural components of the muscle, such as the z-disc, which are important for the proper functioning of the muscle.
evidence: This is supported by the GO term analysis and identification of accessible regions near structural genes.

claim: Open regions of chromatin in MuSCs mostly correspond to genes involved in membrane permeability, adherens junction organization and signalling pathways implicated in regulation of MuSC function.
source: On the other hand, open regions of chromatin in the MuSCs mostly correspond to genes involved in membrane permeability, adherens junction organization and signalling pathways implicated in the regulation of MuSC function (Relaix et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the GO term analysis and citation to Relaix et al., 2021.

claim: Chromatin regions that are accessible in both MuSCs and myofibers correspond to genes crucial for general function of cells such as those involved in mitochondrial transport, regulation of transcription, and regulation of metabolites and energy.
source: The analysis also revealed that chromatin regions that are accessible in both MuSCs and myofibers correspond to genes that are crucial for the general function of cells such as those involved in mitochondrial transport, regulation of transcription, and regulation of metabolites and energy.
evidence: This is supported by the GO term analysis of common peaks.

claim: DMD is a type of muscular dystrophy caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the Dystrophin (DMD) gene.
source: DMD is a type of muscular dystrophy caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the Dystrophin (DMD) gene that encodes for a protein that has a crucial role in muscle structure (Gao and McNally, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao and McNally, 2015.

claim: Dystrophin encodes for a protein that has a crucial role in muscle structure.
source: DMD is a type of muscular dystrophy caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the Dystrophin (DMD) gene that encodes for a protein that has a crucial role in muscle structure (Gao and McNally, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao and McNally, 2015.

claim: Lack of functional dystrophin in DMD leads to unstable and fragile myofibers that continuously need to be regenerated, leading to progressive muscle degeneration.
source: Lack of functional dystrophin in DMD leads to unstable and fragile myofibers that continuously need to be regenerated, in turn leading to progressive muscle degeneration (Gao and McNally, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao and McNally, 2015.

claim: DMD is associated with substantial alterations in chromatin accessibility in myonuclei.
source: We have not only shown that smfATAC-Seq can reliably investigate the chromatin accessibility from a single myofiber of mdx and WT EDL muscle, but through Pearson correlations, PCA and differential peak analysis we have also shown that DMD is associated with substantial alterations in chromatin accessibility in myonuclei.
evidence: This is supported by the differential analysis between mdx and WT myofibers.

claim: A great proportion of peaks common between mdx and WT myofibers are mostly associated with processes involved in muscle structure and organization.
source: Through occupancy and GO term analyses, we have shown that a great proportion of peaks that are common between the mdx and WT myofibers are mostly associated with processes involved in muscle structure and organization.
evidence: This is supported by the GO term analysis of common peaks.

claim: mdx myofibers have more unique peaks compared to WT.
source: However, we have shown that mdx myofibers have more unique peaks compared to the WT, suggesting that chromatin accessibility of myonuclei is increased in the mdx disease model.
evidence: This is supported by the occupancy analysis data.

claim: Chromatin accessibility of myonuclei is increased in the mdx disease model.
source: However, we have shown that mdx myofibers have more unique peaks compared to the WT, suggesting that chromatin accessibility of myonuclei is increased in the mdx disease model.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher number of unique peaks in mdx.

claim: The unique peaks in mdx are associated with biological processes involved in myofiber structure and organization.
source: Our analyses have shown that the unique peaks in mdx are associated with biological processes involved in myofiber structure and organization.
evidence: This is supported by the GO term analysis of unique peaks in mdx.

claim: Unique peaks in WT myofibers are associated with processes mostly involved in energy and metabolism.
source: On the other hand, unique peaks in the WT myofibers are associated with processes mostly involved in energy and metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by the GO term analysis of unique peaks in WT.

claim: It is possible that progressive muscle degeneration due to loss of muscle fiber integrity and stability causes mdx myofibers to compensate by increasing activity of processes involved in muscle structure and organization while WT myofibers retain their activity in metabolism.
source: It is possible that the progressive muscle degeneration due to loss of muscle fiber integrity and stability causes mdx myofibers to compensate by increasing the activity of processes involved in muscle structure and organization while WT myofibers retain their activity in metabolism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences in GO terms between mdx and WT.

claim: The differences in chromatin accessibility between resting and regenerating myofibers and between mdx and WT myofibers are similar.
source: It should be noted that the differences in chromatin accessibility that we have observed between resting and regenerating myofibers and between the mdx and WT myofibers are similar, which could be explained by the degeneration and continuous round of regeneration in the mdx myofibers.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analyses.

claim: The similarity in chromatin accessibility differences between injured vs uninjured and mdx vs WT could be explained by degeneration and continuous rounds of regeneration in mdx myofibers.
source: It should be noted that the differences in chromatin accessibility that we have observed between resting and regenerating myofibers and between the mdx and WT myofibers are similar, which could be explained by the degeneration and continuous round of regeneration in the mdx myofibers.
evidence: This is speculation based on known biology of mdx mice.

claim: smfATAC-Seq is a robust molecular tool that can be used to analyze genome-wide chromatin accessibility of a single myofiber.
source: Overall, smfATAC-Seq is a robust molecular tool that can be used to analyze genome-wide chromatin accessibility of a single myofiber.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The sequencing depth from smfATAC-Seq allows for in-depth analysis, peak calling, quantitative analysis of chromatin accessibility and identification of active enhancers and promoters in a single muscle fiber.
source: The sequencing depth from this approach, allows for in-depth analysis, peak calling, quantitative analysis of chromatin accessibility and to identify active enhancers and promoters in a single muscle fiber.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data and analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: smfATAC-Seq can be used to study epigenetic alterations that occur in muscle fibers during development, diseases, and in response to exercise.
source: smfATAC-Seq can be used to study the epigenetic alterations that occur in muscle fibers during development, diseases, and in response to exercise.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the method.

claim: 65% of the smfATAC-Seq peaks in uninjured myofibers overlap with whole EDL muscle ATAC-Seq.
source: We also analyzed the overlap between the smfATAC-Seq on EDL myofibers with the ATAC-Seq performed on the whole EDL muscle by Ramachandran et al., 2019 (GSM3981673) (Ramachandran et al., 2019). This analysis revealed that 65% of the smfATAC-Seq peaks in the uninjured myofibers overlap with the whole EDL muscle ATAC-Seq (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 3 and comparison with published data.

claim: Accessible chromatin regions are associated with histone marks such as H3K27ac and H3K4me3.
source: Accessible chromatin regions are associated with various histone marks such as H3K27ac and H3K4me3 (Zhang et al., 2015; Berger, 2007; Barrera et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2015; Berger, 2007; Barrera et al., 2008.

claim: The majority of smfATAC-Seq peaks (6090 peaks) were common to H3K27ac peaks present in the entire EDL muscle.
source: Thus, we compared the smfATAC-Seq to publicly available datasets of ChIP-Seq on H3K27ac in EDL muscle that was previously performed by Ramachandran et al., 2019 (GSM3515022, GSM3515023) (Ramachandran et al., 2019). The comparative analysis has revealed that there were only 97 peaks in the smfATAC-Seq that did not overlap with the H3K27ac peaks, while the majority of the peaks, 6090 peaks, were common to the H3K27ac peaks present in the entire EDL muscle (Figure 2—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: This is supported by the Venn diagram shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2K and comparison with published ChIP-Seq data.

claim: The accessible regions assessed by smfATAC-Seq correspond to regions of chromatin marked by histones associated with open chromatin such as H3K27ac.
source: This demonstrates that the accessible regions that are assessed by smfATAC-Seq correspond to the regions of the chromatin marked by histones that are associated with open chromatin such as H3K27ac.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap analysis with H3K27ac ChIP-Seq data.

claim: smfATAC-Seq can robustly measure chromatin accessibility and identify active cis-regulatory elements in a single EDL myofiber.
source: Overall, these analyses suggest that smfATAC-Seq can robustly measure chromatin accessibility and identify active cis-regulatory elements in a single EDL myofiber.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation analyses comparing smfATAC-Seq with other datasets.
